title: Participles: who does it
intro: Turkmen has no word for **who**, **which** or **that** in the middle of a sentence. To describe a noun with a whole action, it turns the verb into a **participle** and puts it before the noun: *kitap okaýan oglan*, the boy (who is) reading a book. You already know a few participles without having called them that: *geçen hepde* (last week: the week that has passed) and *doglan gün* (birthday: the day you were born). This unit builds them up in five steps: `-ýAn` for what is going on, `-An` for what has happened, the possessive on the noun when the noun is the thing done (*meniň okan kitabym*, the book I read), participles used as nouns (*gelenler*, the people who came), and the order of the words before the noun.

sections.title: Step 1: -ýAn, the boy who is reading

blocks.text: **From a sentence to a phrase.** Take a sentence: *Oglan kitap okaýar* (the boy is reading a book). Change `-ýAr` into `-ýAn`, and move the noun to the end: *kitap okaýan oglan*, the boy who is reading a book. The participle stands right before its noun, and everything that belongs to the action (its object, a place, a time) stands before the participle, in the order of a normal sentence.

**What it means.** `-ýAn` describes an action going on now, or one that happens regularly: *kitap okaýan oglan* is the boy reading a book at the moment, or a boy who reads books. Its tense comes from the sentence around it.

The stem changes exactly as it does before `-ýAr` ([A1 unit 6](a1-u06)): *gitmek* → *gidýän*, *etmek* → *edýän*, *öwretmek* → *öwredýän*. The negative is `-mAýAn`: *çilim çekmeýän adam*, a person who doesn't smoke.

items.en: The boy reading a book is my brother.
I know the man who sells carpets at the bazaar.
My friend who lives in Ashgabat is coming tomorrow.
There are few tourists who speak Turkmen.
There are lots of people who don't smoke.

blocks.title: No word for who
blocks.text: English **who** has no match here: not `oglan, kim kitap okaýar`. *Kim* only asks questions. Turn the verb into a participle and put it first: *kitap okaýan oglan*. And not `oglan kitap okaýan`: the noun always comes last.

sections.title: Steps 2 and 3: -An, the guest who came, the book I read

blocks.text: **Step 2: what has happened.** For an action that has happened, or a state that results from it, use `-An`: *-an* or *-en*, just *-n* after a vowel. *Düýn gelen myhman*, the guest who came yesterday; *Aşgabatdan gelen adam*, the man who has come from Ashgabat. As before `-Ar`, a final e becomes ä (*işlän*), and the verbs that soften t do so (*giden, eden, aýdan*).

items.tk: Bu suraty çeken gyz meniň jigim.

items.en: The girl who drew this picture is my little sister.
The guests who came to the wedding danced.
Who's the girl in the red dress?
items.note: Clothes you have on are **put on**: *geýen*. *Geýýän* would be **who (usually) wears**.

blocks.text: **Step 3: the book I read.** The same `-An` can also describe the **thing** the action was done to: the book that was read. Then the doer must be named, and Turkmen names it with a possessive ending **on the noun**: *okan kitabym*, the book I read, literally **my read book**. The genitive pronoun in front is optional, as with any possessive: *(meniň) okan kitabym*.

`-ýAn` works the same way for a place, a time or a thing you use or like: *işleýän ýerim* (the place where I work), *ýaşaýan şäherimiz* (the town we live in), *iň gowy görýän aýdymym* (my favourite song, the song I like best). And the noun takes its case after the possessive, as usual: *beren kitabyňy okadym* (I've read the book you gave me).

items.en: The book I read yesterday is very interesting.
I've read the book you gave me.
The place where I work is in the town centre.
The house we live in is old.

items.tk: Bu meniň iň gowy görýän aýdymym.
items.seg: Bu meniň iň gowy gör|ýän aýdym|ym.
items.en: This is my favourite song.

blocks.title: The ending goes on the noun
blocks.text: *okan kitabym*, not `okanym kitap`, which says **what I read is a book**. And not plain `okan kitap` when you mean **the book I read**: without the possessive nothing says who read it.

blocks.title: One form, two jobs
blocks.text: *Kitap okan oglan*: the boy who read a book; the noun is the doer. *Okan kitabym*: the book I read; the noun is the thing read, and its ending says who. Look at the noun: a possessive ending tells you it is the thing done. The negative of `-An`, *-mAdYk*, comes in [B1 unit 6](b1-u06).

sections.title: Step 4: participles as nouns, those who came

blocks.text: **Drop the noun.** When it is clear who or what you mean, the participle can stand alone and take the endings of a noun. Plural for people: *gelenler* (those who came, the people who came), *okaýanlar* (those who read; readers), *bu ýerde ýaşaýanlar* (the people who live here). Cases as usual: *Gelenlere çaý berdik* (we gave tea to those who came). And on its own, with no ending: *Gelen kim?* (who's the one who has come?)

items.en: Lots of people came to the wedding.
The people who live here speak Turkmen.
We gave tea to those who came.
Is there anyone who knows English?

blocks.text: **With a possessive: what I saw.** A participle with a possessive ending names the thing done, and the ending says who did it: *aýdanym* (what I said), *aýdanyň* (what you said), *görenim* (what I saw). *Aýdanyň dogry*, what you said is right. *Men görenimi aýtdym*, I told (you) what I saw.

items.en: What you said is right.
I told what I saw.
I said what I know.

blocks.title: Someone who…
blocks.text: *Biri* (someone) and *adam* (a person) make handy heads: *bilýän biri* (someone who knows), *tanaýan adamym* (a person I know).

In English a description often follows its noun: **the man who sells carpets at the bazaar**. In Turkmen everything that describes a noun comes **before** it, in the order of a normal sentence, with the participle last: *bazarda haly satýan adam*. To read it, start from the end: the man, who sells, carpets, at the bazaar.

blocks.text: **Adjectives** stay right next to their noun, after the participle: *Aşgabatda ýaşaýan uly doganym* (my older brother who lives in Ashgabat), *iňlis dilini öwredýän ýaş mugallym* (the young teacher who teaches English). The whole phrase then works like a single noun: it can be the subject, take the accusative, or come before a postposition.

blocks.title: Keep the English order out
blocks.text: Not `adam bazarda haly satýan` and not `adam, kim haly satýar`. The noun comes last: *bazarda haly satýan adam*. *Oturan* in the dialogue is **who has sat down**, so **sitting**: like *geýen*, it names a state.

summary: A participle describes a noun with a whole action, and stands right before it: *kitap okaýan oglan*.
`-ýAn` (negative `-mAýAn`) is for what is going on or usual: *Aşgabatda ýaşaýan dostum*; `-An` for what has happened or the state it left: *düýn gelen myhman*, *gyzyl köýnek geýen gyz*.
When the noun is the thing done, its possessive ending says who did it: *(meniň) okan kitabym*, *işleýän ýerim*, *beren kitabyňy*.
A participle can stand alone as a noun: *gelenler* (those who came), *bilýän biri* (someone who knows), *aýdanyň* (what you said).
Everything that describes the noun comes before it, the participle last and adjectives next to the noun: *mekdebimizde iňlis dilini öwredýän ýaş mugallym*.
There is no word for **who** or **that** inside a sentence: not `oglan, kim…`.
